analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 25% minimum tax on income plus unrealized gains for households worth over $100 million.
analysis.headline: The Billionaire Minimum Income Tax Act drew 61 cosponsors but never received a committee hearing or a vote, dying when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require anyone whose net worth exceeds $100 million to pay a minimum tax of 25% on their regular income plus the annual increase in the value of their unsold assets. Tax paid on gains that later prove illusory would be credited back, so the tax works as an early payment rather than a penalty on paper wealth. It also reaches trusts and gifts made within a ten-year window. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: The federal Treasury, and by extension taxpayers generally, since the bill raises revenue from a small group of very wealthy households whose wealth grows without ever being taxed. The bill does not itself direct the new revenue to any specific program.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a minimum tax equal to 25% of a wealthy taxpayer's taxable income plus net unrealized gains — the annual increase in the value of assets they have not sold — on any individual whose net worth exceeds $100 million, capped at 40% of the amount by which net worth exceeds $100 million.
Tax already paid on unrealized gains is credited when those gains are later realized, and any excess is refunded, so the tax functions as a prepayment rather than a double tax.

The bill captures trusts tied to covered taxpayers, counts assets given away during the prior five years when measuring net worth, and treats gifts, charitable bequests, and transfers at death by recent covered taxpayers as taxable gains — closing common ways to move wealth out of the tax's reach.
Taxpayers can elect to pay the tax in five equal annual installments, easing cash-flow strain for those whose wealth is tied up in private companies.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with a net worth above $100 million — roughly the wealthiest sliver of households — plus trusts connected to them. Most of their wealth consists of unsold stock and private assets, so the tax falls on wealth accumulation rather than salaries or sales.

drawbacks.text: Valuing unsold private companies and other non-tradable assets year after year is genuinely difficult. The bill builds an elaborate deferral and valuation regime for these assets, but it hands the Treasury Secretary broad discretion and would generate disputes over appraisals, accounting, and administration.

Owners of illiquid assets — for example a founder whose wealth is almost entirely one private company — can elect a deferral option that puts off most of the tax until the asset is sold or the account resolves, meaning the tax falls hardest and earliest on wealth held in liquid, publicly traded form.

A tax on unrealized gains raises unresolved legal questions, since the federal income tax has historically applied to gains only when they are realized, and such a tax would likely face court challenges on the scope of Congress's taxing power.
The bill raises revenue without directing it to any purpose, so its practical benefit to ordinary people depends entirely on what Congress later chooses to fund.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is straightforward: people whose fortunes grow by hundreds of millions of dollars a year without a sale currently pay little tax, and this bill would change that. The main costs fall on the ultra-wealthy themselves, but the design has real complications — annual valuations of private assets are contentious and the deferral regime is complex. As written, the benefit to the public is potential revenue, not a specific program.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote; it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill in the House on November 29, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
61 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The action history shows no further steps after the committee referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Under the bill, any individual with a net worth over $100 million would owe a minimum tax of 25% on taxable income plus net unrealized gains, capped at 40% of net worth above $100 million.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with more than $100 million in net worth continue to pay tax only when gains are realized, and wealth held in unsold stock, private companies, and trusts continues to grow untaxed. The Treasury forgoes the revenue the bill would have raised.

for.name: Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Billionaire Minimum Income Tax Act in the House.

for.name: 61 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making up its entire list of supporters.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup; the bill sat with no action after referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 61 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican sponsored or supported the bill; the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: These households would owe tax each year on the growth of their wealth, including unsold stock and private assets, rather than only when they sell. The bill also closes escape routes through trusts and gifts made within a ten-year window.

industries.industry: Private wealth management, trusts and estates advisors
industries.note: The bill would require annual asset reporting and valuation for covered taxpayers and would tax gifts and bequests, creating major compliance costs and shrinking the market for structuring wealth to go untaxed.

industries.industry: Private-company founders and owners of illiquid assets
industries.note: The bill allows these taxpayers to elect a deferral option that delays most tax until assets are sold or resolved, softening the impact — but they would still face annual valuations and reporting, and the deferral regime is designed to eliminate the tax advantage of waiting.
